Jest: the Test Runner →

Why Automated Tests?

Poking endpoints by hand with Postman doesn't scale, and it forgets everything the moment you stop.

You've been checking GET/POST /tickets by hand so far — Postman, curl, or the browser. That's a perfectly reasonable way to see whether code you just wrote works right now. It stops being reasonable the moment the API has more than a handful of endpoints: every change means re-clicking through every case you care about, by memory, hoping you don't forget one. Nothing records that "missing subject returns 400" was ever checked at all.

An automated test is that same check, written down as code instead of a manual step: run some code, assert what should be true about the result, and let a tool tell you pass/fail. Once written, it costs nothing to re-run — before every commit, or automatically, forever — and it never forgets a case you already thought to cover.

Not every automated test checks the same amount of the system, though, and the distinction matters enough to name:

  • A unit test exercises one function, in isolation, with no database, no network, no HTTP involved. Fast, and when it fails you know exactly which function is wrong.
  • An integration test (often called an endpoint test for a web API) exercises several layers together through the real interface — an actual HTTP request, routed by Express, handled by a real controller, calling a real service — rather than calling a function directly. Slower than a unit test, but it catches problems a unit test can't: a route wired up wrong, a middleware that never runs, a status code nobody actually checked.

Both kinds are used in this project, starting today — a properly running habit kicks in from Week 3 as services and validators grow, and a fuller endpoint suite (auth, full CRUD flows, the SLA job) arrives in Week 6. But the two pieces of src/ you already have — ticket.service.js, and the whole Express app — are already worth testing exactly as they stand, which is where the next few slides start.
